newsitem.title: SPAIN: Britain likely to get NATO command in Gibraltar.
newsitem.headline: Britain likely to get NATO command in Gibraltar.

text.p: NATO will likely abandon its command in Gibraltar and turn it over to British control, Secretary-General Javier Solana was quoted as saying on Monday.
However, Solana on a visit to Spain did not provide any new clues on the more important question of who will host a NATO command controlling the Straits of Gibraltar.
"Most probably, (the command of Gibraltar) will cease to be a NATO integrated command and will become a strictly British command," Solana was quoted as saying by Spain's Europa Press agency.

Spain, a member of the 16-nation alliance but not of its integrated military command, has said it will join the military structure on condition it can host a NATO command controlling access to the Mediterranean and Iberia via the Straits.
The fourth-tier NATO command in Gibraltar is already run solely by the British.
Spain claims sovereignty over the tiny colony ruled from London for nearly three centuries.
Conservative Spanish Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar is in the midst of a round of consultations with party leaders to clinch parliamentary support for full integration into NATO.
Solana, a former foreign minister of Spain under Socialist rule, has promised to throw his weight behind Madrid to fulfil its conditions for joining NATO's military structure.
"Without a doubt, Spain will have possibilities to have more significant positions in the command structure which we do not have today," Solana said on Monday.
He was in Spain attending an executive session of the Socialist party, headed by former Prime Minister Felipe Gonzalez.
"Spain must have better positions to cooperate in decision-making and in that I can offer help," Solana said.

Gonzalez, now opposition leader, endorsed the government's push for full integration and rejected calls from a fellow opposition member, Communist party leader Julio Anguita, for a referendum on the question of full integration.
"Is it reasonable to ask the Spanish people if we should participate in the command structure of a mission like the one in Bosnia. No it doesn't seem very reasonable to me," Gonzalez said.
Spain voted in a 1986 referendum for limited integration into NATO.
Solana urged Spain to take advantage of opportunities that changes in the alliance present.
"Spain is there when the going is rough -- it has forces deployed in peacekeeping operations -- and I want them to also be there when times are good," he said.
"The magnificent role our soldiers have played in Bosnia must not be forgotten and its justifiable that this role will be accompanied by our participation in a command hierarchy."
